explanations.explanation: God asks why Jerusalem, the city of His people, always turns away. Then He answers it Himself: “They cling to deceit; they refuse to return.” Refuse, friend. That's not a baker who lost the recipe, that's a baker who sees the oven and walks the other way.

It's true. God says of Jerusalem, “They cling to deceit; they refuse to return.” The word is refuse. They aren't confused or lost, they just won't come back. I've had a cookie sheet that wouldn't budge from the rack, but that's nothing next to this.

God says, “They cling to deceit.” Cling means a tight grip, like a toddler holding the last cookie on the plate. They're holding on to the very thing that's leading them away from God. Deceit is the answer in this verse.

I see why you'd go there, since the people were turning to other gods (Jeremiah 7:18). But in this verse, God names something else. He says, “They cling to deceit.” Deceit is what they're gripping here.

Pride is a good guess, because it sounds like what you'd expect from people who won't turn back. But God doesn't use that word in this verse. He says, “They cling to deceit; they refuse to return.” What they're holding on to is deceit.

God says, “Everyone has pursued his own course like a horse charging into battle.” Picture it. A horse at full gallop doesn't stop to ask directions, and it doesn't care what's in front of it. Nobody is asking, “What have I done?” (Jeremiah 8:6).

Sheep wandering is a gentle picture, a little lost and a little clueless. God uses a much louder one here. He says they pursue their own course “like a horse charging into battle.” That horse is going full speed and nobody is reining it in.

A flooding river is a strong picture, but it's not the one God picks. A river gets pushed along by the water behind it. He says, “Everyone has pursued his own course like a horse charging into battle.” This horse is running on purpose.

It's the other way around. God points at the birds that know their seasons, and then says, “…but My people do not know the requirements of the LORD.” The birds have it figured out and the people don't. Ouch.

God says the stork, the turtledove, the swift and the thrush know when to go, “but My people do not know the requirements of the LORD.” So the comparison is there to show the gap. A bird that never read a single word can still keep its schedule. That's the sting of it.

explanations.answer: The lying pen of the scribes
explanations.explanation: God says “the lying pen of the scribes has produced a deception.” The scribes were the writers, and here the pen itself is called a liar. The people said, “We are wise,” while the thing in their hands had been bent. I'd be embarrassed if my stamp did that to a cookie.

explanations.answer: The empty words of the elders
explanations.explanation: Elders do come up in the Bible, but they're not named in this verse. God says what produced the deception was “the lying pen of the scribes.” So the trouble here is in the writing. Pens can lie just as loud as mouths can.

explanations.answer: The false visions of the diviners
explanations.explanation: That's a reasonable guess, since this is a passage about deception. But God doesn't mention diviners here. He says, “…the lying pen of the scribes has produced a deception.” Scribes and their pens are the answer.

God says, “Since they have rejected the word of the LORD, what wisdom do they really have?” They were calling themselves wise while pushing away the very thing wisdom comes from. It's like bragging about your baking while the recipe is in the trash. The word of the LORD is the blank.

The temple mattered a lot to God's people, so I get the pick. But in this verse, God says they “have rejected the word of the LORD.” The word is what they turned away from. And without it, He asks, “what wisdom do they really have?”

Feasts are a fun guess, and I like where your head's at. But this verse says, “Since they have rejected the word of the LORD, what wisdom do they really have?” So the word is the answer. Rejecting it is what leaves their wisdom empty.

explanations.answer: Everyone from the least to the greatest
explanations.explanation: God says, “…from the least of them to the greatest, all are greedy for gain.” That's the whole ladder, bottom rung to top. Nobody gets to point at somebody else and feel clean. He adds that from prophet to priest, all practice deceit.

explanations.answer: Only the rich and the powerful
explanations.explanation: It would be easy to blame just the folks at the top, but God doesn't. He says, “…from the least of them to the greatest, all are greedy for gain.” The least are in it too. So nobody on the ladder is left out.

explanations.answer: Only the merchants in the market
explanations.explanation: Merchants aren't named in this verse at all. God says, “…from the least of them to the greatest, all are greedy for gain.” That's a lot bigger than one group of sellers. It covers everybody.

God says, “They dress the wound of the daughter of My people with very little care.” A wound needs real attention, not a quick wrap and a pat on the head. This one got the pat. Wound is a blank you filled well.

The words are, “Peace, peace,” and then comes the sting: “…when there is no peace at all.” They said it twice, like saying it louder would make it true. It doesn't, friend. Peace is the right word for that second blank.

Debt is a believable guess, since everybody's heard a line like that about money. But this verse is about a wound dressed with very little care. And what they keep saying isn't debt, it's “Peace, peace,” when there is no peace at all.

Victory sounds like something people would shout in a hard moment. But the verse says they were “saying, ‘Peace, peace,’ when there is no peace at all.” So the word that goes in is peace. Victory isn't mentioned.

House is an interesting pick, but this verse isn't about a building. God says they dress the wound of His people with very little care. A wound is what's being covered up, and the covering is the phrase “Peace, peace.”

That's the opposite of what God says. He asks, “Are they ashamed of the abomination they have committed?” and then answers, “No, they have no shame at all; they do not even know how to blush.” So no blushing here. Not even a little pink.

God asks if they're ashamed of the abomination they've committed. Then He says, “No, they have no shame at all; they do not even know how to blush.” A blush usually shows someone knows something is off. These folks showed nothing.

God says, “Whatever I have given them will be lost to them.” That comes right after the harvest is taken away, with no grapes and no figs. Everything they had been handed would slip out of their hands. Lost is the word.
Kept would be a happy ending, but that's not what God says. The verse says, “Whatever I have given them will be lost to them.” It follows a harvest that is taken away. Lost is the word that fits.
Returned sounds hopeful, like a lost wallet coming back in the mail. But God says, “Whatever I have given them will be lost to them.” Nothing comes back here. Lost is the answer.

The voices say, “Gather together, let us flee to the fortified cities and perish there.” Fortified cities are the ones with big walls. They're running to the strongest places they know, and they still say they'll perish. That's a heavy line, so I think it hurts to read.

Mountains are a classic place to run to, so I understand the pick. But these voices say, “Gather together, let us flee to the fortified cities and perish there.” Walled cities are where they plan to go. The mountains aren't in the verse.

Egypt shows up in plenty of Bible stories, so it's a natural guess. But in this verse the voices say, “let us flee to the fortified cities and perish there.” That's where they plan to run. Egypt isn't mentioned.

The voices say, “the LORD our God has doomed us. He has given us poisoned water to drink, because we have sinned against the LORD.” They name the reason out loud. That's a big change from earlier, when nobody asked, “What have I done?” (Jeremiah 8:6).

It's true. These voices say, “He has given us poisoned water to drink, because we have sinned against the LORD.” They admit it right there in the verse. That's different from the people earlier who never asked, “What have I done?” (Jeremiah 8:6).

The voices say, “We hoped for peace, but no good has come, for a time of healing, but there was only terror.” They hoped for healing and got the opposite. That's a hard sentence, and I think it's a sad one. Terror is the answer.
Silence might feel like the quiet after a letdown. But the voices say, “…for a time of healing, but there was only terror.” What came was terror, and it was loud. Silence isn't in the verse.

Darkness is a fair guess for a sad moment like this. But the voices say they hoped “for a time of healing, but there was only terror.” Terror is the word the verse uses. They hoped for good and found something frightening.

The voices say, “The snorting of enemy horses is heard from Dan. At the sound of the neighing of mighty steeds, the whole land quakes.” Dan is in the far north. The horses haven't even arrived and the whole land is already shaking. Imagine hearing that coming from a long way off.

Trumpets would sound dramatic, and I see why you'd think of them. But the verse says, “The snorting of enemy horses is heard from Dan.” Then the neighing of steeds makes the land quake. It's horses that are heard.

Lions would shake anybody up, so that's a good guess. But the voices say, “The snorting of enemy horses is heard from Dan.” They also mention the neighing of mighty steeds. The sound is horses, and they're enemy horses.

explanations.answer: They cannot be charmed and will bite
explanations.explanation: God says, “I will send snakes among you, vipers that cannot be charmed, and they will bite you.” A snake that can be charmed can be calmed down. These can't. No tricks and no music will do the job.

explanations.answer: They will stay out in the desert
explanations.explanation: That would be a relief, but it's not what God says. He says, “I will send snakes among you.” Among them means close, not out in the desert. And these vipers “cannot be charmed, and they will bite you.”

explanations.answer: They will only bite the leaders
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't limit it that way. God says, “I will send snakes among you, vipers that cannot be charmed, and they will bite you.” The word is you, and it's aimed at the people He's speaking about. No leaders-only rule is in the text.
